title: Gate gate
hookLine: gone, gone, gone beyond, gone altogether beyond, awakening, svaha
last: WITHOUT FEAR — NO WALLS, NO FEAR.

cards: Gyatei, gyatei. Near the end of a Japanese morning service, the chanting speeds up and lands on these syllables. They aren't Japanese, and they aren't Chinese either.
They're the last line of the Heart Sutra, and in the Chinese version East Asian temples chant, they were never translated. People chant the sound.
After all the no's and all the emptiness, the sutra ends not with an argument but with something to say out loud.

teach.b: Right after no walls and no fear, the sutra says: so know that the perfection of wisdom is the great mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the mantra that calms all suffering.
Then it gives it, in Sanskrit: "gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā." Gate means gone. Pāragate, gone to the far shore, gone beyond.
Pārasaṃgate, gone completely beyond, all the way over. Bodhi is awakening. And svāhā is an old ritual cry from Indian fire offerings, something like, so be it, or hail.
Gone, gone, gone beyond, gone altogether beyond, awakening, so be it. Scholars still argue about the grammar: gate might mean gone, or it might be calling out to someone, O you who have gone.
Either way the picture is a crossing, the same far shore as the raft three days ago.
Tradition explains the word mantra as man, the mind, and tra, a tool: a tool for the mind. It works less like a sentence you think about and more like a handrail you hold. Now the surprise.
In the Chinese version tradition credits to the pilgrim and translator Xuanzang, every line is translated except this one.
The mantra keeps its sound, written in Chinese characters used for their sound alone.
That's why temples in Japan, Korea and Vietnam still chant a form of the old sounds, each in its own accent.

how: In Zen, Korean, Chinese, Vietnamese and Tibetan communities the Heart Sutra's mantra is chanted in its Sanskrit sound, or a local pronunciation of it, often repeated several times at the end of the sutra.

o: a magic spell that works if said exactly right
a short prayer asking a god for a favor
a sound held and repeated as a tool for the mind

games.q: match each word of the mantra.
p: an old offering cry: so be it

s: the mantra has been translated into Chinese for centuries
Xuanzang kept its sound and wrote it in characters used for sound alone.
svāhā was called out in old Indian fire offerings
it's an exclamation, something like 'so be it' or 'hail'.
scholars fully agree on the mantra's grammar
'gate' may mean 'gone' or may call out 'O you who have gone'.

games.q: you're Xuanzang, translating the Heart Sutra into Chinese. you reach the mantra. what do you do?
o: translate it into plain Chinese, like every other line.
keep its sound, written in characters used only for sound.
leave it out; it isn't an argument.
games.why: the mantra kept its sound in the Chinese, so East Asian Buddhists still chant a form of the Sanskrit sounds.

practice: If you'd like to, say the mantra softly three times, the way it's chanted: gate, gate, pāragate, pārasaṃgate, bodhi, svāhā, feeling the rhythm more than the meaning, with no worry about getting the sounds perfect.
If you'd rather not say it, just listen to it inside. Then let the words go, and rest on the far shore of them, in the quiet after the sound.

wordCard.voice: Mantra. A tool for the mind: sounds held and repeated. The Heart Sutra ends with one, gone, gone, gone beyond.

orig.note: Sanskrit mantra: often explained as man (mind) + tra (tool), a tool for the mind.

carryVoice: Your line: gone beyond. A crossing you can say out loud, in any accent. See you tomorrow.
